title: Invisible Gravity: The Dance of Double Stars Challenges Newton
oneliner: Even after the strictest data cleansing, gravity in wide binary systems stubbornly exceeds Newton's prediction, chipping away at the foundations of standard physics.
description: Three independent samples of binary stars from Gaia data underwent unprecedented scrutiny. But neither the removal of false close encounters nor accounting for hidden companions eliminated the anomaly: at large distances, stars move faster than prescribed by the law of universal gravitation. The dev
abstract: Wide binary stars are an ideal laboratory for testing gravity at extremely low accelerations. By observing their relative speeds, scientists found that beyond a few thousand astronomical units, gravity becomes stronger than Newton predicts—by about 1.3 to 1.6 times. This aligns with MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics). A new study confirms that even meticulous data cleaning and accounting for possible triple systems don’t erase the anomaly. Previous works that denied this effect contained errors due to miscalibration or insufficient data.
threads: Два фигуриста на бескрайнем льду. Их танец едва заметен — но что-то подо льдом разгоняет их быстрее, чем положено. Именно так ведёт себя гравитация в широких двойных звёздах: данные Gaia трижды подтвердили упрямую аномалию. Если эффект реален, тёмная материя может оказаться миражом, а учебники физики затрещат по швам.

title: Robot Tour Guides: Why a Pair Is Better Than One
oneliner: A duo of a robot and a hologram partner makes a museum tour not just a spectacle but a way to absorb facts more deeply, especially for women.
description: Researchers turned the tour into a show: a real robot guide got a holographic assistant. Comparing a solo format, a projection, and a mixed pair on 30 visitors showed that interest was high in all, but recall improved for women with the duo. Participants unanimously preferred the lively conversation
abstract: Scientists have created a museum guide where a physical robot works in tandem with a projected virtual agent, allowing them to simulate lively dialogue between two participants from a single platform. In an experiment with 30 visitors, researchers assessed engagement, experience quality, and information retention under different conversation scenarios. Interestingly, while interest levels remained the same, learning improved only for women when interacting with the hybrid team. This difference is reminiscent of a classroom: some grasp material better in group discussion, while others prefer one-on-one with a teacher. Meanwhile, all participants, regardless of gender, unanimously favored the cheerful tandem over a lone robot, citing the liveliness of the dialogue.

title: Smart Filter for Secret Keys: Autoencoder vs. Noise
oneliner: An autoencoder removes noise from a radio signal, helping two devices obtain a shared reliable secret key.
description: A new method uses an autoencoder—a program that learns to clear noise from a signal, like wiping a fogged-up window. That way, two phones see an identical random picture of the radio channel and can craft a shared secret key, even in heavy interference. The keys turn out stronger, with almost zero e
abstract: Generating secret keys from a radio channel suffers from imperfect reciprocity (differences in measurements on the two sides) due to noise. The authors used a denoising autoencoder (a neural network that cleans data) — it detects the signal structure, removes noise, and restores the original form. The result: far fewer key errors, higher throughput, and better randomness. Think of it as noise-canceling headphones, but for radio waves. This method boosts the physical security of communication channels.

title: How to Pack a Million Shades into a Tiny Box
oneliner: The method packs millions of shades, grouping them like candies in a box, so video chips instantly deliver a smooth picture.
description: Virtual worlds are made of colored dots whose shade depends on the viewing angle. Storing this data is a gluttonous task. Engineers proposed compressing them by grouping similar shades, like candies in a box. The graphics card instantly extracts the average color with a tiny correction, without sacr
abstract: In 3D graphics, spherical harmonics (SH) are often used for view-dependent color. In 3D Gaussian Splatting, this generates a lot of data. The authors compress SH coefficients using GPU-accelerated texture compression (BC1/BC7), grouping primitives by color, which is more efficient than compressing regular textures. Bitrate control is added while preserving fast access—image quality hardly suffers. It’s like packing entire paint palettes instead of each brushstroke individually.

title: Reading the Cosmic Palimpsest: Redshift Tomography of Unresolved Galaxies
oneliner: Scientists have for the first time recovered the redshift distribution for a population of galaxies not seen individually, using multiband background maps and neural network flows.
description: A new study proposes a method for estimating the redshift distribution of unresolved galaxies directly from multiband maps of the cosmic optical background. Using conditional normalizing flows trained on realistic image simulations from Euclid and LSST, the model achieves sub-percent accuracy. The m
abstract: Astrophysicists have for the first time proposed a way to compute redshift distributions (a measure of distance and age) for galaxies that are not individually visible, directly from maps of diffuse background at different wavelengths. A neural network based on normalizing flows, trained on realistic simulations, achieves nearly 1% accuracy—on par with future surveys like Euclid and LSST. The method is robust to missing data and even hints at how much to trust the result. Thus, from light fluctuations, cosmological information can be extracted without needing to resolve each object.
threads: Тусклое свечение космического фона — не брак оптики, а хор из 90% галактик, не видимых поодиночке. Подобно чтению палимпсеста, мы научились разделять этот свет на слои времени и определять расстояние до каждого 'голоса' с точностью менее 1%. Однажды это позволит разглядеть самые первые звёзды Вселенной.

title: Strongly Mixed Worlds: Inflation as a Cosmic Collider
oneliner: Exact solutions for strong field mixing reveal giant signals of heavy particles in the cosmic microwave background, turning the early Universe into an accelerator of ultimate energies.
description: A new mathematical framework for two-field inflationary models with powerful mixing allows precise calculation of the CMB non-Gaussianity, bypassing perturbation theory approximations. Summing effects to all orders, the authors found closed-form expressions for three-point correlators, revealing exp
abstract: Physicists have developed a new method for calculating irregularities in the early Universe when ultrafast expansion (inflation) involved multiple fields. Typically, the main field is considered weakly coupled to others, but here strong transfer of properties between them is examined. The exact approach showed that with strong mixing, deviations from Gaussian statistics can be gigantic—like a small stream merging with a river and turning into a waterfall. This is important for searching for messenger particles from the first moments and explaining the birth of massive black holes.
threads: В первые мгновения после Большого взрыва Вселенная была коллайдером с энергией, недоступной земным технологиям. Её эхо хранит следы тяжёлых частиц. Как мощный блендер, сильное смешивание полей взбило эти сигналы до гигантских амплитуд. Новый математический аппарат позволяет их уловить — и, возможно, выйти на след тёмной материи.

title: Self-Taught Algorithm: How to Hear a Melody from Noise
oneliner: A new adaptive data recovery method tunes its own parameters, achieving near-perfect accuracy even with rough initial errors.
description: A new adaptive method automatically picks parameters to reconstruct a signal from scattered data. It works like a musician tuning an instrument by ear to blend with the orchestra, despite the noise. The algorithm adjusts its internal model on the fly. This is especially valuable when restoring image
abstract: Modern Bayesian signal recovery methods (like compressed sensing) are sensitive to correct model parameter specification. A new adaptive version of the VAMP algorithm uses local EM steps to adjust these parameters on the fly by reusing intermediate statistical moments. It's theoretically shown that this scheme converges to optimal settings, and in experiments with one-bit and multi-bit measurements, it achieves near-oracle accuracy even with deliberately skewed initial conditions. It's as if the detector learns on its own to tell signal from noise, without knowing the signal's characteristics in advance.

title: How to read an enemy in the sky in seconds
oneliner: Combat algorithms learn to make decisions from scraps of data, honestly acknowledging uncertainty.
description: A new air combat algorithm acts like an experienced goalkeeper: from the first patchy radar signals, it predicts the target type and maneuvers, not afraid to admit doubts. In tests — 88% accuracy for class, 93% for intentions.
abstract: In aerial combat, quickly identifying an incoming target and its intentions is life-saving. Current AI needs long observations, but this work proposes a method that operates on short data snippets, using evidential reasoning to handle uncertainty—think of it like a panel of experts voting with confidence levels. It also infers intent by fusing clues over time. Tested on a custom dataset with eight targets, it classified types 88% correctly and predicted intent 93% accurately, enabling split-second tactical decisions.

title: How a Gravitational Trampoline Saves Dust Grains from a Black Hole
oneliner: Curved spacetime acts like a trampoline: statistically flings particles away and rewrites the X-ray variability of black holes.
description: A study of random walks of dust particles in curved spacetime revealed a paradox: the probability of falling into a black hole is lower than in flat space. Geometric drift — the stretching of radial cells — and time dilation flatten the accretion power spectrum at low frequencies, matching observati
abstract: The random motions of dust particles in turbulent matter falling into a black hole can be thought of as wandering on a curved surface. Analysis has shown that because space near the horizon is stretched, a particle has a greater chance of escaping the black hole's vicinity than it would in ordinary space. By modeling thousands of trajectories while considering the accretion disk's structure, we found that X-ray flickering becomes smoother at low frequencies (a time dilation effect) and sharper at high frequencies. This spectrum matches well with data from the Cygnus X-1 binary system, emphasizing the role of geometric wandering in accretion.
threads: Чёрная дыра — не пылесос, а батут: кривизна статистически отбрасывает пылинки к космологическому горизонту. Это открытие меняет взгляд на аккрецию и обещает новый инструмент для проверки общей теории относительности — по временным рядам рентгеновской переменности.

title: Why Genes Disrupt the Family Tree
oneliner: Why gene stories don't match the evolution of species, and how a mathematical model helps unravel the tangle.
description: In evolution, genes don't always follow in the species' footsteps. Random loss of variants or direct exchange between unrelated species muddles the picture. Researchers built a simple model of these transfers to understand how often they create the illusion of a different kinship.
abstract: The study returns to a simple model of horizontal gene transfer (HGT), where events occur randomly at a constant rate (Poisson process). For two and three species, the authors derived probabilities of gene trees and nucleotide patterns. It turns out that distinguishing HGT from incomplete lineage sorting (ILS) is possible, but not always — it's like trying to tell from a single book whether it was gifted or inherited. The results are important for accurate phylogenetic reconstructions.

title: Requiem of a Torn Star: Infrared Excess and the Birth of a Corona
oneliner: Infrared excess from a torn star reveals the secrets of accretion corona birth.
description: Just 40 days after a supermassive black hole tore apart a star in event 2024aepd, infrared telescopes detected an unexpected excess of radiation. Its flat spectrum pointed not to a dust echo but to free-free emission from an extended plasma envelope. Meanwhile, X-ray observations captured the rapid
abstract: Observations of the tidal disruption of a star by a black hole (TDE 2024aepd) in X-ray, ultraviolet, and infrared bands revealed an unexpected excess of infrared emission already by day 40. Its spectrum is too flat to be simply the 'tail' of ultraviolet thermal glow. Free-free emission from a reprocessing gas shell (a kind of hot fog) around the disk is more likely — the third such observation in history. Figuring out how often black hole stellar 'meals' come with such an infrared precursor will help understand the physics of these extreme events.
threads: В считанные недели после того, как чёрная дыра разрывает звезду, рождается горячая корона — область, где фотоны взмывают до рентгеновских энергий, словно оркестр берёт крещендо. Инфракрасный избыток, подобный низкому басу, разносит эхо переработанного излучения. Понимание этих процессов — ключ к разгадке роста сверхмассивных чёрных дыр и рождения галактик.

title: Cosmic Strings in a Nanocomposite: How to See the Echo of the Big Bang
oneliner: Using scanning SQUID microscopy, physicists have for the first time visualized in detail spontaneous quantized vortices in a disordered superconducting nanocomposite MgO/MgB₂ — a laboratory analog of cosmological topological defects.
description: In a recently published study, scientists obtained images of spontaneously arising magnetic vortices in a material where superconducting MgB₂ grains are randomly scattered in a dielectric MgO matrix. Unlike compact Abrikosov vortices, these structures stretch several micrometers and have a bizarrely
abstract: In a second-order phase transition, spontaneous symmetry breaking gives rise to topological defects — in superconductors these are quantized vortices. The authors used a scanning SQUID microscope to observe such spontaneous vortices in a nanocomposite with superconducting proximity effect. They found that in near-zero field, vortices appear randomly, with different polarities, sizes and shapes, and their magnetic field extends further than ordinary Abrikosov vortices (penetration depth from 1 to 10 μm). The vortices are born during cooling due to competition between Josephson coupling and thermal fluctuations, capturing local phase differences at the moment order emerges — like a snapshot of the first instant of the transition.
threads: Космические струны — гипотетические складки пространства-времени — возможно, застыли в первые мгновения после Большого взрыва. Сегодня физики нашли их миниатюрное подобие в куске сверхпроводящей керамики. Запутанные магнитные вихри, самопроизвольно возникшие при охлаждении, — это отпечаток фазового перехода, словно фотография рождения порядка. Изучая их, мы, возможно, поймём, как Вселенная обретала структуру.

title: Magnetic Bridge Through Earth: Relay Boosts Communication
oneliner: Engineers found a way to speed up magnetic communication through the ground using a repeater.
description: Magnetic fields penetrate the ground where radio waves fail. A new method adds a repeater — a device that amplifies the signal — and allows precise calculation of how much faster data transfer becomes. The solutions will be useful in mines, subways, and underwater exploration.
abstract: Magnetically inductive (MI) coupling is useful in mines and underground rivers, but its speed is low. To increase throughput, a cooperative scheme with an amplify-and-forward relay (amplification without decoding) has been proposed. The key novelty is accounting for the arbitrary position and orientation of the relay antenna. Exact formulas for the rate gain and channel bandwidth have been derived. Modeling showed: strategic placement of the relay yields a multiple-fold increase in throughput—even a slight antenna rotation can tip the scales.

title: How a Self-Driving Car Builds a Map from Above
oneliner: Scientists trained a computer to piece together a road map from fragmented snapshots, sifting through possible variations.
description: The computer generates several draft maps and picks the best one, merging camera data as if looking out of different windows. This approach makes lane marking recognition reliable even in bad weather.
abstract: Perceiving the road environment is a crucial task for self-driving cars. A bird’s-eye view (BEV) merges data from cameras into a unified spatial map, but fusing diverse images in complex conditions remains a challenge. The new TVB method tackles this through variational inference: the neural network generates several realistic BEV maps using normalizing flows for plausibility, and then uses an attention mechanism to pick the best one—like an artist selecting the most accurate sketch. Experiments confirm the method's superiority in BEV segmentation on the nuScenes and OPV2V datasets.

title: The Complexity of Crowds: Why Averages Fail
oneliner: CWMMSE measures complexity, seeing not the average picture, but the full diversity of hidden patterns.
description: CWMMSE measures the complexity of trajectory sets by grouping similar paths and assessing not only their entanglement but also the differences between groups. It turns out: a calm ocean is more complex than a stormy one due to hidden diversity of currents, and heart disease reduces not overall chaos
abstract: Groups of time series (ensembles of trajectories) are everywhere: from satellite constellations to medical records. Traditional complexity measures like sample entropy describe individual series, but averaging over the ensemble erases the population structure. The authors developed CWMMSE — a method that first clusters trajectories by behavioral patterns and then computes weighted entropy, separating individual complexity from collective diversity. Surprisingly, a calm ocean can get a higher complexity score than an energetic but uniform one, and heart disease actually reduces diversity, which is missed when averaging.

title: WanSong: Songs from Noise in One Step
oneliner: The WanSong neural network turns random noise into songs up to five minutes long with vocals and instruments.
description: WanSong works like a sculptor: it transforms noise into music by removing the excess step by step. Unlike other models, it creates multi-track songs straight away, with no intermediate stages, and automatically separates vocals and instruments. This makes editing easier.
abstract: WanSong is a pure diffusion model (it generates sound by gradually clearing away noise) that spits out songs up to 5 minutes long in multiple languages. It gives you two tracks right off the bat—vocals and backing—like an artist who paints with both hands at once. It uses step distillation for speed and can be fine-tuned for editing. The result? Commercial-grade quality without those clunky multi-step workflows.

title: Cement's Boson Hum: Terahertz Waves Eavesdrop on Nano-Inhomogeneities
oneliner: For the first time, a boson peak detected in cement gel sheds light on the vibrational life of the nanoworld, linking elastic fluctuations to concrete durability.
description: Scientists have experimentally discovered the boson peak — a universal anomaly in the vibrational spectrum of disordered media — in calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H), the main binding phase of hardened cement. Using terahertz spectroscopy and low-temperature heat capacity measurements, they showed th
abstract: In disordered solids, like hardened cement, there is a universal vibrational anomaly — the boson peak. Using terahertz spectroscopy and low-temperature calorimetry, researchers have systematically studied it for the first time in calcium silicate hydrate (the main component of concrete). The boson peak was found at a frequency of about 1 THz, and its characteristics depend on the calcium-to-silicon ratio. From the peak shape, a correlation length of ~1 nm and a heterogeneity parameter were determined, which is directly related to the material's tendency to creep and its thermal conductivity. It's like a seismogram: by deciphering the 'signal' of the boson peak, we can predict concrete behavior decades ahead, which is critical for creating low-carbon cements.
threads: Представьте барабан, натянутый неравномерно: его звук выдаёт распределение напряжений. Бозонный пик в цементе — такой же «голос» наномира: частота ~1 ТГц раскрывает флуктуации жёсткости на наномасштабе. Управляя этим гулом, мы создадим бетон, который не ползёт веками — и однажды, возможно, отправится на Марс.

title: Ghost Echoes Make Radar More Precise
oneliner: A receiver defect that creates false reflections paradoxically improves radar clarity.
description: Radar signals are split into multiple frequencies. The slightest electronic imbalance spawns phantom copies of targets. Instead of suppressing them, they're used alongside the real ones—accuracy soars.
abstract: In OFDM-based communication and sensing systems, receiver quadrature imbalance (IQI) creates mirror interference — "phantom targets" that confuse the radar. Instead of traditionally compensating the distortion before processing, you can exploit the structure of the distorted signal: every real target leaves a paired trace — direct and mirror, linked through the target coefficient. This leads to an elliptical group detector that directly processes data using two weighted two-dimensional Fourier transforms. The result is sharper detection of even weak targets under strong imbalance. Analogy: it's like recognizing faces in a double-exposed photo, not by fixing the image, but by analyzing the "twins".

title: Radar Sculptor: How Radio Waves Sculpt a Drone's Portrait
oneliner: The technology turns reflected signals into a three-dimensional sculpture, revealing a drone's shape and movement.
description: Scientists trained radar to reconstruct a drone's appearance and notice the slightest changes — down to a light payload. The method outperforms optics in fog and darkness.
abstract: A base station with an antenna array beams radio signals at a drone and from the reflections builds a point cloud — a 3D map from which position, tilt, and shape are extracted. This is a complex inverse problem; the authors proposed the AUGUST method: it uses conditional channel encoding and a diffusion model to reconstruct the point cloud. In simulations, AUGUST gave more detailed restoration than benchmark methods and significantly improved positioning accuracy. Analogy: it's as if a neural network restored a sharp portrait from a blurry radio snapshot, relying on context knowledge.

title: Radar Without Ghosts: A New 'Melody' Against False Targets
oneliner: Engineers composed a radio pulse 'melody' that rids radar of ghost targets while keeping the picture sharp.
description: To cut costs, radar signal processing is 'compressed', but ghost targets appear—like off-key notes in a poor recording. Previous pulse designs gave either clarity with many ghosts or purity at the cost of smearing. The new SC-EFM modulation is a distinct waveform that almost eliminates 'false notes'
abstract: In radar with sub-Nyquist sampling (measuring less often than theory demands), false 'ghost' targets are inevitable due to spectral aliasing. Traditionally, you face a trade-off: LFM (linear frequency modulation) signals give great resolution but spawn ghosts, while HFM (hyperbolic) suppresses them at the cost of blurring nearby targets. The authors propose a compromise—a signal based on Jacobi elliptic functions, whose frequency curvature is smoothly tunable. It simultaneously keeps LFM's sharpness and ghost resilience, outperforming HFM. It’s like tuning a musical instrument: instead of two extremes, one universal waveform.

title: How the Brain Conducts Attention: A Meditation Model
oneliner: A new model explains how the brain manages attention: like an experienced conductor, it learns to quickly notice distractions and gently return to the main focus.
description: Scientists simulated meditation on a computer, identifying four states: focus on breathing, mind wandering, awareness of distraction, and return. Comparing beginners and experts revealed that experienced meditators recognize distractions faster and shift more smoothly. The model links subjective exp
abstract: A three-level model of focused attention meditation has been created within the active inference framework. The bottom level reflects the physiology of brain networks; the middle one generates ‘thoughtseeds’ and evaluates action impulses; the top level, like a conductor, selects them through the global workspace. The key insight: noticing distraction (meta-awareness) arises as a mismatch signal, triggering a return to the object. Training on data from experienced and novice practitioners reproduced empirically observed dynamics. Thus the brain, balancing on a tightrope of attention, continually returns to center.

title: Compressing networks: when roads become points
oneliner: Scientists found a clever way to compress numeric networks: lines become dots, and barely noticeable fluctuations are discarded.
description: A new method for packing numeric maps (like road networks with traffic). First, the map is transformed: roads become nodes, and intersections become edges between them. Then numeric values are decomposed into simple waves, and weak ones are discarded. The rest are encoded very densely. A smoothness
abstract: A new lossy compression method for weighted graphs targets the edge weights. The trick is to turn the original graph into its line graph—where edges become nodes, and connections show adjacency. Then edge weights are seen as a signal on this new graph, smoothed with graph filters (think of it like processing pixels in an image), quantized, and squeezed with entropy coding. They introduce 'edge smoothness,' a simple measure that predicts how compressible the data is. In tests, this beats older matrix-based preprocessing.

title: Flying Radio Mirror: A Drone That Steers Its Own Signal
oneliner: A flying radio mirror adjusts in real time to the drone's shaking, keeping the signal pristine.
description: A prototype smart surface on a drone acts as a self-aiming mirror for radio signals. Even in flight, when the drone shakes, the mirror predicts displacements and instantly reorients itself—keeping the link perfect.
abstract: The first truly working prototype of a drone equipped with a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) has been built—a thin panel that can dynamically redirect radio waves to improve communication. Using onboard sensors and an extended Kalman filter (a motion prediction algorithm), the system instantly adjusts the RIS position to compensate for vibrations and wind gusts. It’s as if a flying drone were holding an active mirror that constantly tilts to keep a sunbeam locked on its target. Tests show this adaptation preserves the communication link’s benefits even under heavy interference, paving the way for reliable aerial relays in 6G networks.

title: How Robots Negotiate the Noisy Airwaves
oneliner: Reliable radio communication between robots improves movement accuracy and saves energy.
description: Random delays in the wireless network confuse robots. Engineers tested different transmission modes in a 5G network: reliable signal delivery improved accuracy by 51.5% compared to the usual approach.
abstract: Collaborative robot control suffers from random delays and packet loss in wireless networks, degrading navigation and obstacle avoidance. By expanding the concept of 'Quality of Control' (QoC), scientists accounted for the impact of motion parameters on delays and reliability. Experiments on a private 5G network showed: optimizing control and communication yields energy efficiency, and the reliable transmission mode (RELIABLE QoS) in ROS 2 improves QoC by 51.5% compared to BEST-EFFORT. It's like moving from a noisy street to a quiet room—robots find it easier to coordinate.

title: Spin from Bend: How Curvature Twists Sound
oneliner: Curvature makes massless phonons acquire angular momentum, turning Hall viscosity into a measurable mechanical torque.
description: In flat crystalline membranes, flexural vibrations do not feel the phonon Hall viscosity—a peculiar, non-dissipative 'fluid' property of media with broken time-reversal symmetry. However, static curvature translates vertical motion into in-plane shear deformation, unlocking the hidden Hall response.
abstract: In flat crystalline membranes, bending modes typically don't feel the phonon Hall viscosity—a quantum coefficient of frictionless transport. But the authors showed that static curvature couples bending to in-plane strain, creating a Hall channel. For shallow isotropic ripples, a stationary torque emerges, proportional to the mean curvature. For a few atomic layers of α-RuCl₃, the estimate yields ~10⁻²² N·m—already within reach of torsion sensors. Just as a curved sheet resists twisting differently than a flat one, nanoscale curvature unlocks access to hidden quantum viscosity.
threads: В крошечной изогнутой мембране из магнитного кристалла звуковые волны не просто колеблются — они начинают вращаться. Кривизна играет роль дирижёра: без неё холловская вязкость — таинственная «смазка», не создающая трения, — остаётся безмолвной. Так рождается постоянный угловой момент, измеримый теми же датчиками, что ловят гравитационные волны. Мы на пороге тепловых гироскопов без движущихся деталей — только геометрия и квантовая фаза.

title: AI Plans Radiation Therapy in Two Minutes
oneliner: Artificial intelligence independently and accurately builds a radiation plan for a cancerous tumor from daily scans—in just two minutes.
description: Scientists have created an AI agent that fully automates the daily preparation for radiation therapy. It processes a CT scan, identifies tumor boundaries, calculates doses, and suggests settings—all in two minutes. A doctor supervises the key steps. As a result, treatment speeds up, the burden on me
abstract: A new system based on a large AI model automates adaptive radiation therapy: in just two minutes, it turns a cone-beam CT scan into a detailed 3D model, outlines the tumor and organs, and then calculates a radiation plan that is as accurate as a manually crafted one. The doctor sets the goals and can adjust key steps—it's not a black box, but a tool under human control. Interestingly, the same model handles head and neck, lung, prostate, and abdominal cancers, and works with both photons and protons.

title: Why photo enhancement software fails on unfamiliar images
oneliner: Photo cleanup programs stumble on unfamiliar images because they take steps in the wrong direction. But a quick tweak with a few examples corrects the course.
description: Photo enhancement software often ruins frames with unusual blur or noise. The culprit isn't a general error, but the algorithm's misdirected steps—it veers off course. By showing it a few examples of proper cleanup, you can adjust its path without a complete overhaul.
abstract: The PnP-PGD method restores images by using neural network denoisers as prior information, but when the data type changes, their accuracy drops. In the work, they measure 'proximal mismatch' — the difference between the applied denoiser and the ideal one for the new task. It turns out that the accumulation error directly depends on this difference. The authors propose adaptation through proximal alignment, rather than just mean squared error. Experiments with deblurring and superresolution show that this approach yields noticeable gains, especially on few-shot examples — as if glasses are adjusted not by a general chart, but directly for your eyesight.

title: A Map That Isn't Afraid to Admit: 'I Don't Know'
oneliner: Robots build a map with guaranteed accuracy, openly admitting where the data is unreliable.
description: Scientists have found a way to fuse data from a group of robots so that the final map directly flags dubious areas. The method works regardless of sensor quality or communication links between the machines.
abstract: To build a reliable shared map, robots exchange minimal data—e-values (statistical confidence estimates). The fusion algorithm dampens the influence of uncertain measurements and caps the group's error budget. This guarantees that the final map is correct a specified proportion of the time, regardless of the communication structure and sensor noise. Yet, where evidence is thin, the map honestly shows both options (free/occupied), leaving unclassified zones. Frequent robot encounters shrink such zones. Simulations back the theory—accuracy hits theoretical limits.

title: How Spite Replenishes Resources
oneliner: When a resource replenishes slowly, spite unexpectedly allows it to recover, then gives way to fairness.
description: In repeated negotiations over a shared resource, the speed of its replenishment decides everything. Rapid growth encourages fairness, slow growth creates a paradoxical cycle: spite temporarily takes over, but this allows the resource to accumulate and fairness to return.
abstract: The availability of renewable resources can determine whether we act fairly or greedily. In a stochastic ultimatum game (one proposes a split, the other accepts or rejects), two players repeatedly divide a resource: successful deals deplete it, rejections allow it to recover. Evolutionary modeling showed that rapid resource growth leads to the dominance of fairness. Slow growth triggers an unexpected loop: greed depletes the stock, but this stimulates recovery, and repeated interactions then encourage honesty. Thus, stinginess paradoxically creates the ground for future generosity.

title: Shadow Symphony: How Data Became a Portrait of a Black Hole
oneliner: The first image of the event horizon is not a photograph but a symphony reconstructed from fragments of a score: algorithms, guided by physical models, filled gaps in the data and turned noise into a portrait of the abyss.
description: In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration unveiled the shadow of the black hole at the center of M87—an image that became a scientific icon. Yet it wasn't a direct photograph: two years were spent transforming sparse signals from eight antennas into a meaningful picture. Every step—from cal
abstract: In 2019, we saw the first image of a black hole's shadow from the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration. However, the extreme noisiness and sparseness of the data meant the same observation allowed many plausible reconstructions. At each processing step, scientists had to choose between alternative algorithms or average results. Analysis of these choices showed: even though the final picture could have looked different, the key feature — the dark spot of the shadow — was almost always preserved. The main achievement isn't a single snapshot, but the demonstration that reasonable variations don't destroy the image.
threads: Когда в 2019 году показали снимок чёрной дыры, многие решили, что это фотография. На самом деле, это симфония, собранная по обрывкам партитуры. Восемь антенн по всей планете уловили лишь несколько «нот» от плазмы вокруг M87*. Алгоритмы, словно дирижёры, достроили мелодию — каждый по-своему. Итог — усреднение трёх версий. Следующее поколение добавит космические «уши», и тогда, возможно, мы услышим голос бездны в полную силу.

title: Where Are You? Radio Waves Know the Answer
oneliner: Like a sensitive ear, your phone picks up the unique pattern of radio waves in a room—and from that, figures out exactly where you're standing.
description: Indoors, a radio signal behaves like a note sung in a concert hall: reflections create a one-of-a-kind melody for each spot. A listener program memorizes these invisible chords and uses them to locate you more precisely than GPS. This technology promises navigation in subways and smart factories.
abstract: Radio signals, bouncing off walls, create unique 'fingerprints' of locations. Learning systems can determine position from these patterns, but fingerprints change with layout, time, device, and settings — like notes sounding different on different instruments in different halls. A new survey shows: the key to reliable localization isn't the algorithm, but how these radio signatures (channel representations) are compressed and described. The survey compares approaches by accuracy, data, and generalizability.

title: How Robots Chart a Course Through a Galaxy of Errors
oneliner: A subtle helm in the digital brain keeps robots from losing their grip, even as the world shifts around them.
description: Robots drop objects when their neural network gets scrambled. Scientists spotted a galaxy in those signals: successful and faulty commands separated like safe and perilous space. So they embedded a helm that steers signals back on course in real time. Now, even with a shaky camera, the grasp holds f
abstract: World Action Models (WAM) that pilot robots tend to wobble when glitches happen. By peering inside the AI's 'brain' with mechanistic interpretability—a deep-dive into neural activations—researchers found that in some architectures, reliability signals line up neatly in the hidden space. That allowed them to craft contrastive 'nudges' that steer the model without any retraining. Harnessing the local linearity of its inner dynamics, they built WA-LQR, a light-touch controller that boosted stability against camera shifts, visual noise, and even switching the robot's grip.

title: How Noise Creates Diversity
oneliner: Random noise can reinforce, not erase, diversity in a population.
description: A new study flips the script: in the Hawks and Doves game, random fluctuations don’t average out behavior but split the population into warriors and peacemakers, preserving this divide for the long haul.
abstract: In evolutionary theory, populations with flexible strategies and those with clear role division were often considered identical. In small groups, random demographic noise can destroy this similarity. The "trembling hand" hypothesis predicted that noise leads to uniformity, but simulations yielded contradictions. Analysis of the hawk-dove game with separation of time scales revealed the mechanism: stochastic effects create long-lived diversity — nature is like a jazz orchestra, where each musician stays true to their part, but together they improvise.

title: Smart Circuits for Clear Signals
oneliner: A new tuning algorithm for radio transmitters turns budget hardware into speed record-holders.
description: When a transmitter has multiple antennas, they need to be matched, otherwise the signal is lost. Scientists developed a method for tuning internal circuits that squeezes maximum speed even from mediocre components.

title: How to Teach AI Not to Confuse Similar MRI Scans
oneliner: Scientists have proposed a method that helps artificial intelligence analyze medical images more accurately, even when they look identical.
description: Typically, during training, AI compares paired data and treats everything else as different. But in medicine, two scans can be very similar even though they belong to different patients. This confuses the AI, leading to errors. The new MseaCL system uses doctors' text reports to understand how simil
abstract: Contrastive learning (a method where the model pulls similar items closer and pushes dissimilar ones apart) often stumbles in medicine by treating any unpaired scans and reports as completely unrelated. This creates false negatives, especially when patients have similar diagnoses. The authors proposed factoring in the semantic similarity of textual reports to soften this problem. Tested on pediatric brain MRIs, this approach boosted molecular tumor classification quality by over 22% in AUC — like a teacher who stops assuming everyone not at the same desk has nothing in common, and instead peeks at their interests.

title: The Milky Way Symphony: Why Star Clocks Tick at Different Speeds
oneliner: A new study of 736 stars reveals: the ratio of yttrium to magnesium is a temperamental chronometer, its pace depending on the star's birthplace and metallicity.
description: To circumvent the challenge of directly determining stellar ages, astronomers turned to 'chemical clocks'—pairs of elements whose ratio changes over time. Yttrium and magnesium are among the most promising pairs: magnesium disperses rapidly after supernova explosions, while yttrium slowly accumulate
abstract: A study of 736 stars with precisely measured ages revealed: the ratio of yttrium to magnesium (a chemical clock: yttrium comes from slow-burning stars, magnesium from fast ones) depends differently on age in different parts of the Galaxy. For stars of solar metallicity, young ones are poor in yttrium, old ones rich; at supersolar metallicity, the difference smooths out, the clock slows down. This reflects the uneven history of star formation and disk enrichment.
threads: Звёздный хронометр оказался с географией: во внешнем диске Галактики химические часы на иттрии и магнии спешат, а в толстом — еле ползут. Это открытие рушит миф об универсальном методе датировки и рисует Млечный Путь как оркестр, где каждая секция играет в своём темпе. В будущем многомерные модели машинного обучения восстановят всю историю Галактики по этим разноголосым партитурам.

title: The Cosmic Score is Silent: Dark Matter and Neutrinos Don't Play a Duet
oneliner: The most sensitive cosmic 'ear' hasn't heard a duet: a new analysis of the Lyman-alpha forest sets a record limit on the interaction between dark matter and neutrinos, sweeping aside recent hypotheses.
description: Comparing data from Keck and VLT telescopes with model spectra from hydrodynamic simulations, scientists used a neural network emulator and Bayesian analysis. The upper limit uνχ ≤ 1.5×10⁻⁸ is a hundred times stricter than previously allowed. Dark matter and neutrinos barely notice each other: they
abstract: By analyzing the 'Lyman-alpha forest' (patterns of hydrogen absorption lines in quasar spectra), the authors modeled cosmological evolution involving dark matter interacting with neutrinos. They obtained the tightest limit to date on the strength of such interaction: the coupling parameter does not exceed 1.5×10⁻⁸. This closes previous hints of a non-zero effect and shows that a popular method of rescaling warm dark matter constraints overestimates the strictness here. As it turns out, the 'conversants' from the dark sector hardly exchange any signals.
threads: Миллиарды лет свет квазаров нёс сквозь космос ноты водородной партитуры. Астрофизики прислушались, надеясь уловить дуэт тёмной материи и нейтрино. Но расслышали лишь абсолютное молчание: взаимодействие оказалось как минимум в сотню раз слабее, чем предполагали смелые гипотезы. Этот предел не просто отсекает модные теории — он заставляет по-новому взглянуть на скрытую жизнь Вселенной.

title: Gene Map Predicts Breast Cancer Outcomes
oneliner: A mathematical cartographer drew a map of the genetic city and found the neighborhood where aggressive breast cancer becomes vulnerable.
description: For a thousand women with breast cancer, scientists created an activity map of genes—each gene like a house, its work the life inside. The mathematical cartographer revealed hidden neighborhoods invisible to standard tests. It turned out that patients from 'quiet' neighborhoods with aggressive cance
abstract: Using the Mapper algorithm (a method for analyzing the shape of data) on gene expression from over 1000 breast cancer patients, scientists uncovered a hidden network structure where proximity to high-risk regions predicted worse survival. A surprise was a subgroup of basal-like cancer with favorable outcomes, linked to a specific gene signature susceptible to therapy. This shows that the geometry of molecular data—like an invisible terrain—holds critical prognostic information overlooked by traditional methods.

title: How Galactic Dust Traps Heat from Invisible Black Holes
oneliner: The spin of primordial black holes boosts interstellar dust heating, and rotation helps to tighten constraints on their contribution to dark matter.
description: Primordial black holes are elegant dark matter candidates. Their Hawking radiation heats cosmic dust, offering a new way to assess their fraction. For the first time, spin and halo profiles are systematically accounted for: rotation dramatically boosts heating, and the isothermal profile sets a limi
abstract: The rotation of primordial black holes (candidates for dark matter) has been accounted for, which amplifies the heating of interstellar dust by Hawking radiation (the energy emitted by black holes). A comparison of five dark matter halo models showed that the isothermal profile imposes the strictest constraints, and a higher spin rules out a larger fraction of black holes. Silicate dust grains heat up more than graphite ones, and for rapidly spinning holes, the dark matter fraction is limited to 0.01%. Analogy: spin turns a black hole into an invisible space heater for cosmic dust.
threads: Межзвёздная пыль — триллионы микротермометров, разбросанных по Галактике. Они чутко реагируют на малейший нагрев, выдавая местоположение испаряющихся чёрных дыр. Учёт спина показал: даже слабое вращение умножает излучение и затягивает петлю ограничений. Возможно, скоро инфракрасные карты неба станут окном в природу тёмной материи.

title: A Colorful World Through a Single Pixel
oneliner: Adaptive mask switching helps a single pixel distinguish hundreds of shades without expensive optics.
description: Cameras that distinguish hundreds of shades are expensive. A new approach captures such images with a simple sensor: the measurement sequence is tailored to the scene, boosting clarity in visible and near-infrared light.
abstract: To get detailed spectral images, you usually need expensive specialized sensors. An alternative is single-pixel imaging (SPI) with deep optical coding, but its quality suffers due to rigid pattern fixation. The authors proposed a flexible method where the order of Hadamard basis functions (light patterns) is dynamically rearranged depending on the scene, optimizing the capture of hundreds of frames. It's like tuning a musical instrument for a specific melody rather than playing from a single score. Tests on real setups showed a noticeable increase in image clarity in visible and near-infrared ranges.

title: World in Flickers: How a Camera Assembles an Image from Flashes
oneliner: From a stream of flickers, scientists assembled a detailed picture of the Earth's surface.
description: Regular cameras capture frames. Event-based ones only detect changes in light. Scientists have shown how to assemble a sharp image from these changes, like a puzzle of light shards. Tests on the ISS confirmed: the method distinguishes clouds, islands, and landscape.
abstract: Event cameras only capture moments when brightness changes, producing a sparse data stream instead of continuous video. In this new work, that stream was treated as a synthetic-aperture problem: much like radar, the camera's motion lets it collect 'depth-different' projections of a single static scene. By building a linear model and applying regularization, scientists recovered the logarithmic brightness field—shedding noise and revealing large-scale structure where conventional methods would drown in texture details. The result: crisp geometry from a chaos of flashes.

title: Why Not Every Contact Leads to Illness
oneliner: A new model accounts for infection depending on the amount of virus, which changes over time.
description: Scientists created a model where infection depends on the 'age of infection'—the time since the virus entered the body. This age determines how much virus can be transmitted upon contact. The larger the dose, the higher the chance of getting sick. Such a model predicts epidemic development more accu
abstract: Researchers have developed an infection spread model that, for the first time, explicitly separates exposure to the pathogen from actual infection. In classical models, any contact with an infected individual is considered a potential transmission, but here, infection occurs with a probability depending on the viral load of the contact. To achieve this, an 'age' structure of infection is introduced—essentially the duration of illness, which indirectly describes the amount of virus in the carrier. This allows for more accurate prediction of epidemic dynamics. Much like not every spark ignites a fire: it all depends on the amount of fuel.

title: Lightweight AI for Space Communications: More Accurate and Efficient
oneliner: A tiny AI model predicts radio signal distortions on a satellite, using almost no power.
description: Interference disrupts satellite communications. A new power-efficient AI running directly on board accurately catches signal distortions with minimal energy consumption. This will bring internet to the most remote corners.
abstract: In future 6G networks, satellites will be part of the infrastructure, but powerful AI channel estimation algorithms aren't suitable for them due to energy constraints. Researchers have developed a lightweight convolutional neural network that accounts for the peculiarities of satellite channels: high predictability and Doppler shifts (frequency shifts). The model requires 29 times fewer operations and 27% fewer parameters than typical solutions, while providing a more accurate estimate (MSE). It's like a microchip that bypasses a bulky computer: efficient AI will improve connectivity in orbit without wasting energy.

title: Robot Juggler: Synchronized Play with a Human
oneliner: Engineers have taught a robot to catch and throw balls in rhythm with a human, like an experienced circus duo.
description: The robot has mastered paired juggling with a human: it catches and tosses balls, predicting their flight in a split second. Even beginners achieved record-breaking synchronicity.
abstract: A new study tackles the challenge of human-robot collaborative juggling — a dynamic exchange of objects where accurate perception (tracking ball positions), timing, and feedback are critical. The team developed a real-time planning and control architecture that includes predictive ball tracking and adaptive trajectory optimization. In an experiment with 8 participants, the system set a record: a three-ball cascade with 20 consecutive catches, doubling the previous best. Interestingly, even beginners adapted quickly — much like dance partners learning to feel each other's rhythm. These technologies bring us closer to a future where robots become reliable teammates in physical tasks.

title: Icy Origins: Most Hot Jupiters Come from the Cold
oneliner: Chemical analysis of the atmospheres of nine hot Jupiters revealed their icy origins: at least six were born far from the star, beyond the snow line, and ended up in close orbits due to gravitational catastrophes.
description: Scientists simulated planet formation in a protoplanetary disk, tracing the path of carbon and oxygen across the snow lines of water and carbon dioxide. Comparison with real spectra of hot Jupiters showed that most began life in the outer cold of the disk and then underwent violent migration. This d
abstract: Astronomers have discovered that the chemical composition of hot Jupiters' atmospheres can indicate where they formed. In a protoplanetary disk, different substances freeze at different distances from the star (at the so-called snow lines). By simulating the formation of nine such planets, taking into account dust drift, accretion, and migration, they found that at least six of them were born beyond the water snow line. Comparing these data with orbital parameters, scientists suggested that most systems experienced dynamical scattering and tidal evolution. Just as a dialect reveals a person's origin, the atmospheric 'accent' of a planet tells the story of its journey toward the star.
threads: Большинство горячих юпитеров, пышущих жаром у самого лица своих звёзд, на самом деле носят ледяное прошлое. Химия их атмосфер — как клеймо на перегретом паровозе, сошедшем с рельсов: она выдает рождение далеко за снеговой чертой, где вода замерзала в лёд. Это значит, что системы пережили гравитационные катастрофы, расшвырявшие планеты к звёздам. Скоро мы сможем читать эти химические летописи для тысяч миров.

title: Neural Cartographer: Recovering Invisible Laws
oneliner: A hybrid method recovers hidden dynamics, like a cartographer creating an accurate map from fragmentary landmarks.
description: Scientists have created a method that completes partial equations in physics and biology. Known laws serve as landmarks, and a neural network, like a cartographer, draws uncharted regions by learning from available measurements. This improves forecast accuracy while keeping the model interpretable.
abstract: Many dynamic systems are described by differential equations, but some equations are unknown and measurements are incomplete. A hybrid approach: known physics stays explicit, while unknown components are modeled by a neural network. The method alternately estimates hidden states using RTS smoothing (a statistical method) and trains the network on smoothed trajectories, allowing model completion from data scraps. As a result, long-term forecasts improve and interpretability is maintained—like an archaeologist reconstructing a vessel from shards without guesswork.

title: Underwater Postman Robot with Charging
oneliner: An underwater robot uses light to locate sensors and smartly manages its energy — either recharging them or just collecting data.
description: The robot spots sensors by their faint glow and then decides: if the battery is almost dead, it recharges; if it's half-full, it first gathers data then tops it up; if full, it simply reads. This strategy extends the underwater network’s lifespan and conserves the robot’s own power. A simple equatio
abstract: Researchers proposed using a mobile robot (AUV) that simultaneously transmits data and wirelessly charges sensors. The SA-OPS strategy was developed: depending on the sensor's charge, one of three actions is selected — urgent charging, data transmission with charging, or transmission only. Simulations showed an improved balance between the robot's energy consumption and the overall energy health of the network compared to baseline approaches. It turns out the charging threshold can be approximated with a simple heuristic — much like an experienced driver knows when to refuel to avoid stalling.

title: How to fish out a friend's voice from a noisy conversation
oneliner: A new competition teaches algorithms to fish out a friend's voice from real hubbub, not studio silence — with interruptions, echo, and the hiss of a coffee maker.
description: You recorded a group's chatter, but you want to hear just one voice. Until now, such systems were trained on artificial mixes without echo or noise. Now the REAL-TSE Challenge has launched — a competition on real recordings with interruptions and street noise. Participants create an algorithm that,
abstract: The task of extracting a target speaker's speech (TSE) from a multi-voice mixture is one of the key challenges for hearing aids and voice assistants. The new REAL-TSE competition is the first to use not studio recordings, but real conversations in English and Chinese with natural overlaps, echo, noise, and different recording channels. It offers two modes: online (instant processing) and offline (with full context). Results are evaluated on speech intelligibility, voice similarity, and accuracy of speaker activity detection. This is a major step from lab tests to real life.

title: Atmospheric Palimpsest: Sulfur as the Key to Exoplanet Interiors
oneliner: Sulfur dioxide in the atmospheres of distant planets, contrary to expectations, does not vanish under the onslaught of stellar radiation, but serves as a reliable indicator of redox processes deep below the surface.
description: Joint modeling of planetary evolution and chemical kinetics has shown that although the bulk atmosphere of rocky exoplanets inherits the composition of gases released from the mantle, the star's photochemistry radically alters the upper layers. Yet sulfur dioxide (SO₂) accumulates there to concentra
abstract: Scientists studied how the interiors and atmospheres of rocky exoplanets interact. Using evolutionary modeling (PROTEUS) and chemical calculations, they showed that the overall atmospheric composition—reducing (hydrogen-rich) or oxidizing (carbon dioxide-dominated)—is determined by the redox state of the mantle and degassing history. Photochemistry under stellar radiation only alters the upper layers, but it creates a bright indicator: sulfur dioxide (SO₂), especially noticeable with intermediate and oxidized interiors. Synthetic spectra showed that these SO₂ signatures in the infrared (4 and 7-9 μm) will reach ~60 and ~100 ppm, then return to background levels of ~30 and ~50 ppm.
threads: Палимпсест атмосферы: звезда переписывает химию, но сера сопротивляется. SO₂ на экзопланетах как древняя строка, проступающая сквозь новый текст. Мантия выдыхает газы, фотохимия скраблит пергамент, а мы видим только глубокий след окисления. Так геология становится видимой в телескоп. Будущая миссия Ariel превратит это в карту недр.

title: How arterial pulse moves fluid in the brain
oneliner: A simplified model shows how pulsing arteries act as pumps, pushing cleansing fluid through spongy tissue.
description: A mathematical model of fluid flow around brain arteries boiled down to a single equation. Flexible walls and a porous structure are key to efficient brain waste clearance.
abstract: Periarterial spaces (channels around brain arteries) are crucial for brain clearance. Their walls are flexible and porous, and the flow of cerebrospinal fluid is driven by vessel pulsations. This work accounts for porous resistance (via a Darcy–Brinkman term) and fluid-structure interaction with a compliant wall. The problem is reduced to a single nonlinear equation for pressure, yielding analytical solutions for weak waves and paving the way for parametric studies.

title: The Illusion of Accuracy: How AI Testing in Acoustics Misleads
oneliner: The testing method matters more than the algorithm: data leakage creates an illusion of accurate acoustic prediction.
description: High AI accuracy in acoustics is often an illusion caused by data leakage during testing. Honest validation crushes it severalfold, but even then, algorithms accurately measure loudness and decay time, and most importantly, masterfully reconstruct the sound field between sensors.
abstract: The authors showed that the high accuracy of AI models for room acoustics is often illusory. Under honest validation (splitting by positions, without 'hints' from test points), R² dropped from 0.81 to 0.09–0.57. The hybrid neural network used the impulse response as a fingerprint of the location rather than acoustic information. In realistic conditions, models still better predict sound strength and reverberation, and high numbers return for interpolation between measured points—a separate useful task.

title: A Smart Navigator That Doesn’t Trust Itself
oneliner: A neural network notices when a standard tracking algorithm starts making mistakes and retrains itself in a fraction of a second without human help.
description: A self‑learning module has been built into drone and satellite tracking software. It senses that the old rules are no longer working and instantly adapts, making predictions more accurate in any unstable environment.
abstract: The Kalman filter is a mathematical tool for estimating a system's state from incomplete and noisy data (like a satellite's position). Its neural network-based variant, KalmanNet, boosts accuracy but loses reliability when the environment changes. Researchers proposed CASA-KalmanNet, an architecture with a CPDNet module that monitors internal degradation signals and triggers adaptive fine-tuning on the fly, without new labeled data. In tests, the method outperformed alternatives and nearly matched ideal classical filters, like an immune system spotting a threat just in time.

title: How AI Stopped Mixing Up Sounds in a Script
oneliner: An AI conductor keeps things in line: a new method forces audio generators to follow the script more strictly.
description: When a neural network turns text into sound, it easily messes up the order of events. The solution is a judge model that listens to the recording and checks it against the script. Based on its assessments, it teaches the generator not to confuse a ring with a door slam. The new S3Bench test confirme
abstract: Text-to-audio models often stumble on instructions that involve multiple events in a specific order. The fix? Using audio-aware large language models (ALLMs) as 'judges' that check for the presence and sequence of sounds. Their assessments, coupled with human verification, generate training pairs for direct preference optimization (DPO), sharpening accuracy without sacrificing quality. Like a strict music critic scoring a composition, the ALLM catches missed or misplaced events. The method boosted completeness and temporal consistency on the new S3Bench benchmark.

title: Radio Waves Paint Portraits of Obstacles
oneliner: Radio signal distortions reveal a precise 'portrait' of an obstacle — its size, shape, and distance.
description: A radio signal bending around a building creates a pattern of peaks and fades — a radio portrait. Scientists have developed a method that reads these invisible 'brushstrokes' and reconstructs the exact appearance, size, and location of the obstacle. It uses only ordinary frequencies, yet accuracy re
abstract: Engineers have developed a model that uses radio wave diffraction — their ability to bend around obstacles — to accurately 'feel' objects in an environment. Maximum likelihood methods can reconstruct the shape, distance, and signal source directions of an obstacle, with the theoretical accuracy limit set by the Cramér-Rao bound. Interestingly, the model is universal across frequencies and propagation regimes (from near field to far field), and estimation performance approaches the ideal already at moderate signal levels. The diffraction pattern scales like a hologram: change the frequency or object size, and the pattern transforms predictably.

title: Imitation Drone Dodges Black Holes of Uncertainty
oneliner: The drone copies an ace's flight, but knows where the 'black holes' are: it automatically steers clear of zones where even a tiny mistake leads to a crash.
description: The algorithm teaches to copy the best maneuvers but adds insurance: if reality differs from training, the drone itself realizes the old path is dangerous and builds a safe detour, avoiding 'black hole' zones. This makes delivery and rescue drones invulnerable to surprises.
abstract: Imitation learning suffers from distribution shifts: when conditions change, a trained agent may act unsafely. A new approach combines a Taylor series-based method (TaSIL) with robust adaptive control to handle two types of shifts—those caused by the agent's policy and those caused by environmental uncertainty. It’s like a versatile pilot who accounts for both their own flying style and the whims of the weather. Drone tests confirmed it reliably avoids dangerous zones even under unpredictable conditions.

title: Space modules heal wounds without commands
oneliner: Modular satellites can now close punctures on their own, as if sealing a wound.
description: A self-repair algorithm for cube-shaped module satellites. When punctured, surviving blocks, like cells in a wound, crawl toward the hole and restore the shape from memory — without blueprints or commands. The more modules, the more precise the reassembly.
abstract: A system of modules is like a network: a break severs connections. Old methods require spare parts or a rigid plan. The new algorithm copies wound healing: modules hear the ‘cries for help’ of broken neighbors, converge to the tears, and then return to their places by memory — without a center or knowledge of exact coordinates. In tests on a simulator with 160 modules, even after randomly losing 30% of pieces, more than 80% of the healthy ones were able to reconnect into a single whole, and on larger structures the result is even better. Imagine: an orbital station that ‘heals’ a breach by itself, just like skin.

title: Untangling Layered Radio Modulation: The TSDN Method
oneliner: A neural network archaeologist separates hidden layers of signal encoding.
description: Engineers built the TSDN neural network, which acts like an archaeologist, separating tangled layers of modulation in radio signals. It shifts the signal into logarithmic space, where layers add instead of multiply, and learns to accurately reconstruct even unfamiliar combinations, staying locked on
abstract: In future communication and sensing systems, automatically recognizing composite modulations (CM), where one signal type is nested inside another, is crucial. The main challenge is the semantic entanglement of layers: useful information is all mixed up, like blended paints. The authors proposed TSDN — a network with logarithmic mapping and a learnable geometric transformation that 'unravels' this mixture. The method achieves over 93% accuracy even for modulation types unknown during training and works at signal levels below 4 dB, outperforming existing approaches. This is a step toward receivers that adapt to new protocols without training — like a universal translator for radio waves.

title: Frugal Radar: Powering Up Only When the Target Slips Away
oneliner: By predicting motion, the system turns off its transmitter and saves up to 50% energy—like astronomers waiting for an exoplanet transit.
description: Future 6G networks will merge data transmission and radar. Constant scanning is costly, but there's a solution: akin to astronomical transit observations, measurements are taken only when uncertainty arises. An algorithm, honed on the Apollo missions, halves power consumption without sacrificing lin
abstract: In future 6G networks, communication and radar sensing will work together, but constant radar emission consumes a lot of energy. A signal shaping method is proposed that activates sensing only when needed, based on two indicators from a Kalman filter: confidence in the target position estimate and measurement reliability. This saves energy while maintaining communication quality and tracking accuracy, much like smart headlights that adaptively illuminate the road.

title: The Musical Horizon: How a Song Gains Dimension
oneliner: Artificial intelligence turns music into an emotional 360-degree video.
description: The algorithm breaks down a song into emotions in four-bar steps, then creates a panoramic video that changes with the mood. The user finds themselves inside an animated painting born from sound.
abstract: The new Bring Music The Horizon system creates 360-degree videos that follow the emotional curve of a song in real time. First, the algorithm predicts mood (from negative to positive) and energy (from calm to excited) every four bars from the notes. Then, like an artist, it turns these emotional labels into visual images, and then 'stitches' them into a smooth panoramic video. It's like an orchestra conductor directing not just the sound but an imagined visual sequence—only now it's all automatic.

title: AI Judges Listen Not with Ears, but with Labels
oneliner: AI speech assessment systems often rely on textual cues rather than the sound itself.
description: Experiments show that speech assessment algorithms ignore the sound and focus on textual labels. Like a critic who reads the menu but doesn’t taste the dish, such judges score based on the description. Even when their scores match human evaluations, they cannot be trusted in high-stakes tests.
abstract: Large audio-language models increasingly evaluate speech as automatic judges. But high agreement with humans doesn't guarantee the model is actually listening: it might rely on protocol-based hints. Three scenarios were tested: evaluation based on acoustic feature text descriptions, with a reference, and A/B comparison. Many models are vulnerable: incorrect labels drop accuracy to 0.10 (chance level), and in A/B tests some always pick a fixed position, ignoring swaps. Like a taster who only reads the label—correlation with humans exists, but understanding does not.
